quiz.reason: Duplicate of n37 (same claim, same fact): keep one. The lines' fear fact (11 of 36 felt strong or extreme fear) would balance whichever is kept.

item.statement: In a big trial for hard-to-treat depression, psilocybin's benefit was still clear after 12 weeks.
item.why: By 12 weeks, the gap between the full dose and a tiny dose could be chance, though the full dose did better at 3 weeks. Everyone in that trial of 233 adults got some psilocybin, so it compared doses.

quiz.reason: The why's second sentence moves the 'could probably tell they had taken psilocybin' limit, which belongs to the US niacin trial in the short, onto the big trial, where everyone took psilocybin. Near-duplicate of n40.
'Heavily' matches the lines' 'heaviest-use group' (more than 50 times), and the why gives the definition and the 6-fold contrast.

item.statement: Teen cannabis use has been shown to lower IQ later in life.
item.why: Not shown either way: in one New Zealand study, people dependent on cannabis for years lost about 6 IQ points, but other differences between people could explain it. Twin studies of mostly lighter teenage use found no clear extra loss, though they could miss a small one.

quiz.reason: The original why is accurate but never says 'not shown either way', ends on the first team's defence of its result, and leaves out the twin studies, the only evidence in the lines about teenage use. A reader can't see why the answer is Myth.
'Serotonin marker' is vague, but it is the lines' own term.
A risk fact, not advice. Myth rests on one lab study of six to nine people; the why says so.
Mixing card, but framed as a risk fact: feeling less does not mean less MDMA in the blood.

item.statement: Among emergency patients who'd taken GHB or GBL, those who'd also had alcohol more often went to critical care.
item.why: Of those kept in hospital, 55 in 100 with alcohol went to critical care, against 22 in 100 without. Alcohol use was reported, not measured, and the amounts weren't known.

quiz.reason: The statement applied the finding to everyone who took GHB or GBL with alcohol; the lines only compare patients who came to emergency care.
Myth rests on one study of 11 people; the why keeps that.

item.statement: Taking benzodiazepines for a long time has been shown to cause dementia.
item.why: Not shown: neither of two studies could rule out that early dementia, which can bring worry and poor sleep, led to the prescriptions. Quebec records linked long use to Alzheimer's, but a Seattle study that tested people found no clear link with the heaviest use.

quiz.reason: The original calls Fact what the lines only say could not be ruled out (early dementia leading to the prescriptions), and it avoids the question people actually ask. Rewritten around the lines' answer, 'Not known'.

item.statement: In doctors' reports of health problems after laughing gas, most people had numbness or tingling.
item.why: Of 100 people in published reports, 80 had numbness or tingling and 58 had trouble walking. Not all used it for fun: 25 had been given it in surgery.

quiz.reason: The lines give 80 of 100 with numbness or tingling but never say it was the most common problem, and not every problem is listed. 'Most people had' is what the lines support.

True and supported, but close to self-evident: once having drugs for your own use is no longer a crime, those arrests drop out of the count. The same claim's lines hold a stronger card: past-year use barely moved while lifetime use rose from 8 to 12 in 100, and treatment grew at the same time.

item.statement: With opioids, take-home fentanyl strips showed fentanyl about as often as staff tests on site.
item.why: In British Columbia, 90 in 100 take-home results on opioids showed fentanyl, and 89 in 100 on site; with meth and cocaine, home strips showed it far more often, though the authors think most extra positives were false. The two groups tested different samples, and no lab checked which results were right.

quiz.reason: 'Trained' staff is not in the lines, which say only 'staff'. Without the authors' view that most extra home positives on meth and cocaine were false, readers may take home strips to be better at finding fentanyl.

item.statement: Once people stop using ecstasy, their test scores bounce back, research shows.
item.why: Nobody knows yet: in a few small studies, people who had stopped for at least 6 months scored about the same as people still using, and both scored lower than people who had never used. But these compared different people, not the same people over time.

quiz.reason: The lines speak only of 'scores' and never name memory. If the page's question is about memory, the original wording can stand.
Myth rests on one lab study; the why says so.

item.statement: The LSD chromosome scare began with LSD added to blood cells in a lab dish.
item.why: The cells came from just two people, plus a patient with no 'before' test; studies up to 1970 found no clear rise in broken chromosomes after pure LSD. But those were small and looked only at blood cells under a microscope, not sperm or eggs.

quiz.reason: The original why gives only limits and leaves out the answer itself (no clear rise after pure LSD), so it can read as if the scare still stands.
Same claim and finding as n51, framed the opposite way: keep one.
The lines never mention violent crime; Myth follows only from 'strongest for selling drugs and property crime'.
Duplicate of n1; this version is a little fuller.
Near-duplicate of n2; this card's why is correct.
Supported, but few forum readers believe pills always contain MDMA, and the tests end around 2002. The interest is all in the history.
Same claim and finding as n33: keep one.

item.statement: At one US autopsy centre, deaths nobody thought were from drugs almost never turned out to be drug deaths.
item.why: Drug tests showed about 49 in 100 of the 237 deaths nobody thought were from drugs actually were, and about 10 in 100 suspected drug deaths had another cause. Only two US places have been studied, so others may differ.

quiz.reason: The 49 in 100 comes from deaths at one autopsy centre. The original statement claims it for deaths in general, which the lines cannot support.
